oneSentence: A type of AI that produces new content such as text, images, audio or video from patterns learned from many examples.
plainExplanation:
Generative AI takes an input, often called a prompt, and produces content. The input might be a sentence, question, sketch, reference image, audio clip or a mix. The output can be text, pictures, speech, music, code or video.

Under the surface is a mathematical model trained on examples. Training adjusts internal numbers so the model captures statistical patterns in the examples. When a person gives a prompt, the model uses those patterns to produce an output conditioned on that input. A large language model is one kind of model used to generate or transform text. Generative AI is the broader category and also covers other media.

This differs from systems used mainly to sort, score or predict labels, such as “fraud risk” or “spam”. Those are often called predictive AI. Generative AI produces content. One system can do both, so the boundary is not always neat.

The output can be useful, but it can also be wrong, biased, misleading or made-up. It does not verify facts without another step or tool. Human review, source checking and safe use rules matter, especially for public communication or official work.

everydayAnalogy.title: Drafting a shipping note from past examples
everydayAnalogy.story: At a busy port, a clerk has read thousands of past shipping manifests and delivery notes. A supervisor says, "Write a short delivery summary for 240 boxes of soap, 12 pallets, arriving from Mombasa to Muscat." The clerk quickly produces a plausible summary in the usual format and wording. It looks useful, but the clerk might still copy the wrong vessel name, invent a container code, or miss an unusual handling instruction unless someone checks it against the real records.

mapping.analogyElement: The clerk who has seen many past documents
mapping.aiElement: A trained model built from many examples

mapping.analogyElement: Checking against real records before sending

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A human clerk may understand the actual shipment, ask clarifying questions and consult current records. A generative model does not reliably do that by itself; it generates from learned patterns, not from direct awareness of the real shipment unless connected to trusted data and tools.

visual.title: How generative AI turns a prompt into content
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to say that generative AI uses learned patterns from training data to generate new content from a prompt, and that the output still needs checking.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. Box 1 shows many small icons for documents, images and audio clips labelled 'training examples'. Box 2 shows a larger box labelled 'trained model learns patterns'. Box 3 shows a prompt card entering the model, for example 'Draft a three-line situation summary'. Box 4 shows several possible outputs: a paragraph, an image thumbnail and a speaker icon, followed by a small warning badge labelled 'review needed'.

steps.label: Training examples
steps.explanation: The system is trained on many examples of content, such as text, images or audio.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a cluster of small file, image and waveform icons on the left with the label 'many examples'.

steps.label: Pattern learning
steps.explanation: Training adjusts the model so it captures statistical patterns: which pieces often fit together.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a central rounded rectangle labelled 'model' with subtle internal dots or nodes; connect the example cluster to it with a thick arrow.

steps.label: Prompt
steps.explanation: A user provides an input, such as instructions, questions or reference material.
steps.visualInstruction: Place a prompt card above or before the model with sample text and an arrow into the model.

steps.label: Generated content
steps.explanation: The model produces a new output that matches learned patterns, such as text, an image or audio.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw three small output cards on the right for text, image and audio, with a warning icon and label 'check accuracy and appropriateness' beneath them.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping each stage reveals a short tooltip with one sentence: examples feed training, training shapes the model, the prompt guides generation, and outputs require review.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains generative AI as a four-stage flow. First, many examples of content such as documents, images and audio are used in training. Second, a model is trained to capture statistical patterns in those examples. Third, a user gives a prompt, such as a request for a summary or an image. Fourth, the model generates new content based on those patterns. A note at the end says the result can be useful but still needs human checking for accuracy, safety and suitability.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box flow replaces animation. Arrows show the same sequence from training examples to trained model to prompt to generated content, with a final visible note saying review is needed.

workedExample.scenario: A user wants a short event announcement in two languages.
workedExample.input: Prompt: 'Write a 60-word public event notice in English and French: coastal clean-up on Saturday 14 September, 09:00 to 11:00, meeting at Coral Bay Community Centre, bring water and sun protection, free entry.'
process: The prompt gives the task, length, languages and event details.
The model generates wording by combining patterns it learned from many public notices and bilingual texts.
It produces an English version and a French version that look fluent and properly formatted.
A human reviewer checks the date, time, place name and French wording before publication.
workedExample.result: Draft output includes a clear 60-word English notice and a matching French notice, but the reviewer corrects one translated phrase and adds the organiser's approved contact line.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A communications officer drafts a first public-facing situation summary from approved, non-sensitive source notes after a flood response meeting.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Generative AI can speed up first drafts, suggest clearer wording and produce versions for different audiences, but staff still need to verify facts, tone, legal sensitivity and consistency with approved information.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not paste confidential, personal, protection-sensitive, security-sensitive or unapproved operational information into a public AI service. Use only approved tools and keep human oversight before any release.

whyItMatters: Non-specialists hear this term in procurement, policy, media and workplace tools. Knowing what it actually does helps you ask better questions about accuracy, risk, cost, privacy, authorship, oversight and whether it is even the right tool.
whereYouMayHearIt: news about chatbots and image tools

commonMisconceptions.correction: Chatbots are one use case. Generative systems can also create images, audio, video, code and other content formats.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the output sounds confident, it is probably correct.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Fluent wording comes from pattern generation, not guaranteed truth. A model can produce convincing errors or invented details.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Generative AI always creates something completely original.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The output is newly generated, but it is shaped by patterns in training data and prompts. That raises questions about similarity, copying and attribution in some cases.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Generative AI and predictive AI are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Predictive AI usually estimates a label, score or category, while generative AI produces content. Some systems combine both, which is why people mix them up.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Generative AI is software that can make new text, pictures, audio or video after you give it a prompt.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Generative AI uses trained machine-learning models, often deep-learning models, to estimate the probability of content sequences or structures and then sample or construct outputs conditioned on an input prompt or reference signal.

keyTakeaway: Generative AI makes new content from learned patterns, not guaranteed facts.

quickCheck.question: Which example best matches generative AI?
options: A system that assigns each email a spam score
A system that writes a draft meeting summary from bullet points
A spreadsheet formula that adds monthly totals
A rule-based tool that blocks files over a size limit
quickCheck.explanation: Generative AI produces new content, such as a draft summary. The spam score example is predictive, and the other two are conventional software or rule-based automation.

searchKeywords: ai that creates text and images
contested: The broad idea is widely used, but the exact boundary is not fully settled. Some people use the term narrowly for systems that generate media, while others include a wider range of content-producing models and tools.

issues.problem: The statement that the model generates “a likely continuation or variation” is text-centric and does not accurately describe all listed forms of generative AI. A prompt-to-image or prompt-to-audio output need not be a continuation or variation of the input.
issues.fix: Replace it with: “When a person gives a prompt, the model uses those patterns to produce an output conditioned on that input.”

issues.problem: The explanation distinguishes generative AI from predictive AI but not from a large language model. Readers may wrongly treat the terms as interchangeable, despite generative AI being the broader category described here.
issues.fix: Add: “A large language model is one kind of model used to generate or transform text. Generative AI is the broader category and also covers other media.”

issues.problem: The claimed left-to-right four-box flow places the trained model before the prompt, while also saying that the prompt enters the model. Arrows from model to prompt would misrepresent the data flow.
issues.fix: Use: “A flow diagram shows training examples pointing to a trained model. A prompt card also points into the model. The model points to possible text, image and audio outputs, followed by a warning badge labelled ‘review needed’.”

issues.problem: The sequence “trained model to prompt” again implies that the model produces or passes data to the prompt. The prompt should feed into the trained model.
issues.fix: Use: “A static diagram shows training examples feeding model training, then a prompt feeding the trained model and generated content leaving it. A final visible note says review is needed.”

issues.problem: “A 60-word public event notice in English and French” does not say whether the limit is 60 words in total or 60 words for each language. The date also omits a year, so the claim that 14 September is a Saturday cannot be validated for publication.

This is not a checkable worked result because neither notice is shown. No arithmetic can be performed: zero notice words are provided to count, so the claimed 60-word English notice cannot be verified. The French correspondence and corrected phrase also cannot be checked. A human must supply both drafts, state whether each must contain 60 words, count them, and identify the correction.
